newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Abbey says acquisition prices high.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Abbey says acquisition prices high.

text.p: Abbey National Plc will not now expand its life assurance and long-term savings business by acquisition after missing out earlier this year in the auction for mutual life company Scottish Amicable, Abbey chief executive Peter Birch said on Tuesday.

"We missed out on ScotAm this year," Birch said in an interview, "We're growing very strongly organically and we think the cost of acquisition is very high. So we will try now to grow organically rather than by acquisition."
Birch said funds under management had grown strongly, rising about 50 percent to over 9.0 billion stg over the last year.
"The life division is doing extraordinarily well," Birch said.
Earlier, Abbey National announced a 23 percent rise in profits to 687 million stg in the first half compared to 558m million in the same period last year.
It raised its dividend 17 percent to 10.2 pence per share.

Birch said he did not rule out acquisitions in other parts of the Abbey's business, noting it had recently completed the takeover of financial services group Cater Allen to boost its treasury and offshore segments.
But he said that a repetition of Abbey's 1996 acquisition of National & Provincial building society was unlikely to be repeated because of the current high price of building society assets.
Birch agreed that, despite the disappearance of many large societies there are still some that would be worth acquiring, "But there are a lot of people interested in them too," he said.

The Abbey's continuing acquisitive nature was confirmed when the bank said it will reduce its current 9.2 percent tier one capital ratio to around 7.25 percent by the end of the next three years while maintaining progressive dividends.
"We are still acquisitive and we'll continue to use capital to make acquisitions and pay our shareholders well," Birch said.

Abbey increased provisions against bad debts to 70 million stg in the half compared to 49 million stg in the first half of last year but Birch said this was a function of good growth in unsecured lending and he remained comfortable about credit quality.
Birch admitted that margins were under pressure in the mortgage and savings market in the first half and the bank reported a net outflow of 300 million stg of liquid savings in the first half.
Its market share of 0.6 percent of the increase of outstanding UK mortgages was well below its 14.3 percent market share of the stock.
"The market is very competitive and we've performed reasonably well but not as well as we would have liked," Birch said.
He said the market had been a false one during the first half of the year with billions of pounds of deposits locked in accounts at converting building societies.
Birch said house prices are expected to rise by around eight percent this year in the UK, slowing to five percent next year.
